name: How do design-build teams handle long-lead items?

mainEntity.name: What happens if windows, cabinetry, or specialty finishes take a long time to order?
mainEntity.text: What happens if windows, cabinetry, or specialty finishes take a long time to order?

acceptedAnswer.text: Long-lead items can disrupt even well-planned projects if they are not identified early. Specialty windows, custom cabinetry, imported finishes, appliances, and certain mechanical components can take weeks or months to arrive. A disciplined design-build team should flag these items during preconstruction and coordinate approvals early enough to protect the schedule. The best process starts with a procurement review during budgeting and design. That means the team looks at which products have long manufacture times and whether those decisions need to be finalized before construction begins. If they do, the owner should know that early. This matters a lot in luxury residential projects because custom selections can dramatically affect timing. If a critical item is delayed, the crew may have to resequence work, which can increase costs and extend the schedule. Ask your builder which items are on the long-lead list and when they need to be approved. A good preconstruction plan should include a procurement timeline, not just a construction start date. That gives you a much more realistic view of the project and helps prevent avoidable delays once work is underway.
acceptedAnswer.description: Good design-build teams identify long-lead items during preconstruction, approve them early, and build the schedule around delivery dates. If they wait too long, construction can stall while materials are ordered. The preconstruction phase should flag these items before work starts so procurement and sequencing stay aligned.
